hook.text: Two random humans share 99.9% of their DNA. The 0.1% difference doesn't map onto racial categories.

buildup.text: Human genetic diversity is greatest within Africa because that's where our species has existed the longest.

discovery.text: More genetic variation exists within any one continent than between continents. Race has no genetic basis.

twist.text: Traits like skin color vary gradually across geography, not in sharp boundaries. There are no pure races.

climax.text: Genetics confirms what anthropology long argued: human races are social inventions, not biological realities.

punchline.text: Our differences are real; racial categories are not.

quiz.question: Where is human genetic diversity greatest?
options: Within Africa, where humans have existed longest

details.summary: Human genetic diversity is remarkably low compared to other species — all humans share about 99.9% of their DNA. Most genetic variation exists within continental populations, not between them, making traditional racial classifications genetically meaningless.
details.whyItMatters: The fact that humans are genetically more similar than most species demolishes the biological basis for racism. Greater variation exists within Africa alone than between Africa and the rest of the world.
takeaways: Humans share about 99.9% of their DNA with each other
Most genetic variation exists within populations, not between them
Traditional racial categories have no valid genetic basis

faq.question: Why is human genetic diversity so low?
faq.answer: A population bottleneck roughly 70,000 years ago may have reduced our ancestors to as few as 10,000 individuals. All non-African populations descend from a small group that left Africa, further reducing diversity. Our species is young, and our genetic homogeneity reflects a recent common origin.

faq.question: If race is not genetic, why do populations look different?
faq.answer: Visible traits like skin color represent tiny fractions of the genome shaped by local environmental selection. These traits vary clinally along geographic gradients with no natural boundaries between groups. Our eyes notice surface differences while genetics reveals overwhelming similarity beneath.
